Wewush eats in my mind like smoke on the wind. Tell me, spirit: how many are there at Wewush, and how far do they sit from our fires? Do they ask for seed to plant or for bread to keep them through the lean?  

If they are near and many will die without help, we will spare some grain—yet not so much that our own children go hungry in winter. I would send them enough for one season and a few handfuls of seed, and we would send one of our people to learn from them and to make friendship. Is that what you would have me do?

Spirit, your voice touches my sleep and I wake with it heavy on my chest. Tell me plainly—how many at Wewush go hungry? Are they close enough that our people can walk there without leaving our stores bare? Will they meet us with open hands, not with knives?

We have much grain upon our shelves; I do not fear a single sack to help a neighbour. But land grows tired if we give wrong, and winter comes to all. If you would have me send grain, show me the hungry and their number, that I may give what is wise and keep my people safe.

Wewush. The name comes like a gull cry in my head, spirit. Tell me true — where sits this village, and how many bellies go empty? Are they friends or strangers who have raided?  

I do not throw away the store. We have grain enough to feed my people through many winters. If Wewush needs, I will give, but a little at a time: seed grain to plant, and food to mend the weak, not so much that my folk will go bare in lean weeks. I would ask them to send a person here with news, or leave a token of promise, or trade what they can.  

Will you watch the road while men go with grain? Or will you tell me if helping them will bring hurt?

Spirit, your voice comes at night; I do not trust night voices until I have seen with my own eyes.

Tell me plainly — where is this Joawethom, and how many are hungry there? Do they welcome strangers, or do their people take by spear? Will giving grain make them our friends or make us weak?

If what you say is true, I will not send all our food. We are bound to be fair, and we are not foolish. I will send two able adults as an envoy with a modest gift of grain and a roll of cloth — enough to feed a few families for a little while and to show our hand. They will go to learn who these neighbours are and whether more help is needed. If they prove honest and grateful, we will share more. If they lie or take by force, we will bring our people home and shut our doors.

Spirit, your word sits in my bones, but I will not give without knowing.

Tell me: how near is Wewush? Do their people hunger from bad luck, or from war and stealing? Are they folk who would repay with craft, with work, or with war in time of want? How many mouths must be fed?

If they are plain neighbours and not wolves, I will send grain. We have store enough; I would send a sack or five, and two steady men with a gift and my voice of warning: take only what you need, and in autumn return what you can—work, fish, hide, or a song for our feast. If the spirit says they are true, I will set those men going at dawn.

Tell me: where is Joawethom? How near? How many there are hungry, and why they fail — flood, raid, lazy fields? Show me the road in my dream if you would have us go.
